Nvidia smashes expectations with $115.8 billion in sales in its first results without Jensen Huang, at the end of a dark day on Wall Street

On Tuesday, November 17, after the close, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly sales, more than double a year ago and well above the $109 billion expected. The stock gained up to nearly 5% after hours, a few hours after a session that sent the S&P 500 to its lowest level since July [1][8][4].
Adjusted earnings reached $2.68 per share, versus $2.48 expected, and net income $65.3 billion, up 105% year on year [1]. Data centers, which sell AI chips, account for $107.6 billion (+110%) [1].

For the current quarter, Nvidia is targeting about $130 billion, with no data center sales in China [1][3]. The group has stopped shipping its authorized Hopper chips there, which had brought in about $2.4 billion in the previous quarter [10].

This is the first report since Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 [3]. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who became interim CEO, says it is "business as usual" and raised expected sales growth for fiscal 2027-2028 from 70% to 75% [1][2].
Huang had said he would be "honored" to return if asked [11]. Board chairman Harvey Jones replied that the board had no intention of reinstating him; the search for a permanent CEO continues [2].
After hours, the stock rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, and up to 4.8% according to Bloomberg [7][8]. On Wednesday morning, South Korea's Kospi index gained up to 3.3% [9].

On Tuesday, the S&P 500 lost 1.03%, to 7,340.53 points, its lowest in five months; the Dow Jones fell 1.64%, to 50,759.42 [4]. Salesforce lost more than 9%, Intuit and ServiceNow between 6% and 7% [6][12].

Key takeaway: Nvidia sells most of the chips that run AI, and its numbers show whether the data center race is slowing down. The answer: no [1][2]. For analyst Daniela Hathorn, it is "a solid response to concerns" about demand [2].

But the leadership crisis is not over. Huang left over personal conduct "contrary to the code of conduct", after allegations of affairs, including one with an alleged spy for China, according to the BBC [3][2]. Nvidia is creating a committee for national security and global trade [2].

Wall Street remains nervous: on Tuesday, outages on sensitive networks, including a classified NSA network, also weighed on markets, according to CNBC [5]. On Thursday, Anthropic's stock market debut, raising up to $64 billion, will be a new test for AI [12].

If you have a "world" or US index fund in your stock savings plan or life insurance policy, Nvidia is one of its largest holdings: its results move your savings. And China is still excluded from its forecasts, a sign that the tech rivalry between Washington and Beijing continues.

Rare earths: Malaysia lifts its ban on raw ore exports for France, with a French-Malaysian plant expected in early 2027

On Tuesday, November 17, in Kuala Lumpur, Emmanuel Macron and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership". Malaysia agrees to export certain raw rare earths to France, and a French-Malaysian separation plant is due to start in early 2027 [1][2][3].

This is Emmanuel Macron's first visit to Malaysia since 2017. Agreements were signed on the energy transition, semiconductors and defense, as well as a memorandum of understanding on critical minerals [1][3].
Anwar Ibrahim explained that his country agreed to export certain raw rare earths to France because Paris has committed to working with Kuala Lumpur on processing them [1].
This is an exception: since 2024, Malaysia has banned exports of its raw rare earths to protect its resources and develop its industry [1][4].

The flagship project brings together France's Carester and Malaysia's Malaco Mining: a ten-year joint venture and a separation plant in the state of Perak, with a capacity of about 13,000 tonnes per year, due to start in early 2027 [5][3].

According to the Élysée, the memorandum provides for technology transfers, exchange of expertise and access to critical minerals; the partnership also covers artificial intelligence, undersea cables and civil nuclear power [6].
Kuala Lumpur presents this text as its first critical minerals agreement with a European country; an energy component was also signed between Malaysian power company Tenaga Nasional and EDF [7][8].
The two countries also discussed cooperation against "hybrid threats" [2].
Key takeaway: France wants to depend less on China, the world's largest producer of rare earths, and Emmanuel Macron presents this project as a way to protect French industrial jobs [3][5].

Rare earths are metals used in particular for electric motor magnets and electronics. The challenge is not only extracting them, but separating and refining them: that is the step the Perak plant targets, and the one Malaysia wants to develop at home [5][4].

The deal with Malaysia is a two-way exchange: Kuala Lumpur opens up its ores, and Paris brings its refining know-how to help the country move up the value chain. France is to receive part of the exported raw materials [1].
It is still a project: no figures have been published on the volumes reserved for France, and the 2027 timeline still has to be met [7][9].

Your electric car, your phone or a wind turbine contain magnets made with rare earths, almost always processed in China. Diversifying suppliers limits the risk of shortages or price spikes if Beijing turns off the tap, and may help keep factories and jobs in France.

news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.title: Trump in Asia: in Manila, the Quad signs rare earth agreements to depend less on China, on the eve of the meeting with Xi and Putin
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.summa: On Tuesday, November 17, in Manila, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit, Donald Trump convened the Quad with Narendra Modi (India), Anthony Albanese (Australia) and Sanae Takaichi (Japan). The four countries signed agreements on critical minerals and rare earths, and denounced "economic coercion", without naming China [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.point: This is the first meeting of Quad leaders in about two years, and Donald Trump's first in this format. It was held on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN summit, just before his departure for China [1][2].

The four countries signed several agreements on critical minerals and rare earths, including a common "framework", so that none of them depends on a single foreign supplier that could exert pressure. India and the United States also signed their own agreement [1].

Donald Trump promised that the United States would have "everything we need" in rare earths within ten months: "We're going to catch up in ten months." According to CNN, however, the data show the country is still far behind China [1][2].
In their joint statement, the leaders express "serious concerns" about "economic coercion", notably through "arbitrary export restrictions", and reject any change to the status quo by force [1][3].

Other announcements include: a partnership on undersea cables, extended to power cables thanks to Australia, cooperation on maritime surveillance, cyber and counterterrorism, and a Quad business leaders forum that India will host in 2027 [3].
Narendra Modi summed up the logic: Australian mines, Japanese recycling, American know-how and Indian factories can together strengthen supply chains [3]. Donald Trump called him a "tough man" [4].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.why.0: Key takeaway: before sitting down with Xi Jinping, Donald Trump wanted to show that he could count on his Asian allies to reduce dependence on Chinese rare earths [1][2].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.why.1: Rare earths are metals essential for magnets in electric cars, wind turbines, smartphones and weapons. China dominates their production. Last year, in the middle of a trade dispute with Washington, it restricted its exports, before an agreement in June and a one-year pause in its controls [1].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.why.2: The rest of the trip is busy. On Wednesday, November 18, Donald Trump has lunch with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos at Malacañang Palace, then flies to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit, which brings together Asia-Pacific economies [5]. There, he is expected to extend a trade truce that limits tariffs on Chinese goods and is due to expire soon [5].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.why.3: In recent months, the tariffs Donald Trump imposed on India had weakened the group, according to analysts [2]. Seeing it united again sends a signal to Beijing, a few hours before the three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin [6].
news.2026-11-18-trump-quad-manille.forMe: Rare earths are in your phone, your future electric car and the wind turbines that produce your electricity. If major countries manage to depend less on China, the risk of shortages and price spikes for these products goes down. But catching up will take time.

DR Congo: six months on, Ebola is spreading twice as fast as in West Africa, and Barrick sends employees at its Kibali gold mine home

On Tuesday, November 17, the WHO convened its emergency committee on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DR Congo for the third time. More than 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths, and still 400 to 500 new cases per week. According to Reuters, infections are rising twice as fast as during the record outbreak in West Africa [1][3].

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was declared on May 15. According to government data cited by Reuters, more than 11,000 people have been infected and more than 5,500 have died since then [1].
The US CDC counts 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths as of November 14, and reports cases linked to this outbreak in Kampala, the capital of Uganda [7].

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus counted 67 affected health zones in eight provinces. Two thirds of confirmed deaths occur outside treatment centers, a sign that patients are identified too late [3].
Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths. Seven in ten infected children under five have died, a "terrible" toll according to Tedros [3].

In Haut-Uele, next to Ituri, Barrick has put some non-essential employees and contractors at the Kibali gold mine on leave, after two Ebola deaths in a nearby community. According to an internal memo dated November 12, no employee has been exposed and production continues normally [5].
Health workers are on strike over working conditions and unpaid wages, some since August. Of the $2.9 billion pledged for the response, less than half has been paid, according to Africa CDC [1][6].

Key takeaway: this is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak in history, and it is not under control. It is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DR Congo, and it dwarfs the 2018-2020 one, which caused 3,481 cases and 2,299 deaths [1][2].

Africa CDC, the African Union's health agency, is worried. Its director, Jean Kaseya, warned on November 15 that, if it is not stopped, it will be "the worst Ebola outbreak". He advises against closing borders: "people will take informal routes, and they will cross anyway" [6].

The economy is mainly hit at the bottom: according to Reuters, no large industrial mine has had cases, but the outbreak is hitting artisanal mines [5]. Barrick's memo shows that large groups are getting ready [5].

The response is held back by insecurity and money: according to Doctors Without Borders, supplies are not reaching hotspots outside Ituri [1]. Tedros notes, however, that rapid transmission has been stopped in most of the first hotspots, and trials of vaccines specific to the Bundibugyo strain are due to start [3][4].

The risk for you in France remains very low. But the virus has crossed borders: Kenya has reported nine cases linked to an imported patient, including two deaths, and Nigeria one case [3]. If you travel to the region, get informed before you leave. On the economic side, a spread to large mines would weigh on gold supply [5].
Coming weeks
Start of trials for two vaccines designed against the Bundibugyo strain, announced by the WHO [3][4].

Nvidia: markets had bet on an 8% jump, the stock does only half that despite record results, proof that on the stock market you play against expectations

Before Nvidia's results on Tuesday, November 17, options were pricing in a move of about 8% in the stock, or more than $300 billion in value at stake. Despite sales of $115.8 billion, well above expectations, the stock rose only between 2% and nearly 5% after hours [3][4][7].

Options, contracts that bet on a stock rising or falling, anticipated a swing of about 8.5% in either direction after the report, according to Reuters cited by Quartz, or a move of about $335 billion in market value [1].
According to Benzinga, it was the largest expected move ahead of Nvidia results since August 2024 [2]. Invezz spoke of a "$300 billion bet" on an 8% swing [3].

Reported results: $115.84 billion in sales, versus $109.10 billion expected, and $2.68 in adjusted earnings per share, versus $2.48 [4]. The forecast for the current quarter, $130 billion, also beats the consensus of about $125 billion [6].

The stock gained about 2% after hours according to CNBC [4], nearly 4% to $161.57 according to CBS [5], and up to 4.8% according to Bloomberg [7]. A move smaller than all the estimates derived from options, FinanceFeeds notes [8].
Before the results, the stock had closed at $156.14, in a week weighed down by Jensen Huang's departure [9].
The stock remains about 35% below its October peak, close to $240 [10].
Key takeaway: on the stock market, a good number is not enough. A stock's price already reflects what investors expect; only a surprise relative to those expectations moves the price [11][12].

There are even two levels of expectations: the official analyst consensus, and what big investors really hope for, sometimes called the "whisper" number. In August 2024, Nvidia beat the consensus but fell well short of the most optimistic forecasts: the stock dropped [11][12].

Nvidia carries so much weight in the indices that its results move the whole market. On Wednesday morning, Nasdaq 100 futures gained 0.8% and South Korea's Kospi index up to 3.3%, driven by chipmakers [7][13].
This time, the modest rise is also explained by uncertainty over leadership: the board rules out Jensen Huang's return and has not yet found a permanent CEO [14].

If you follow a stock ahead of its results, first look at what is expected, not just the reported number. A company can announce a record and see its share price fall. And if you have a US or "world" index fund, Nvidia is a very large holding in it: these sessions move your savings.

How it works: the move expected by options

An option gives the right to buy or sell a stock at a set price, up to a given date. The more investors expect a big shake-up, the more expensive these options become. By comparing their prices, you can work out the "implied" move the market anticipates after an event. For Nvidia, it was about 8% to 8.5% [1][3]. If the stock moves less than expected, as here, those who paid a lot to protect themselves against a big swing lose their stake, even if the news is good [8].
Past cases: when results matter less than expectations
February 22, 2024

Nvidia reports $22.1 billion in quarterly sales, versus about $20.4 billion expected. The stock jumps 16.4%, to $785.38, and gains $277 billion in value in a single session, a Wall Street record; the S&P 500 rises 2.11% [15].
When the surprise is strong, Nvidia lifts the whole market [15].
August 28, 2024

Nvidia reports $30.04 billion in sales, versus $29 billion expected, and forecasts $32.5 billion. But it is its smallest surprise since February 2023, and the most optimistic analysts were aiming for $37.9 billion: the stock loses 6% after hours, to $118 [11][12].
Beating the consensus is not enough when real expectations are higher [11].
March 2000

Cisco, which makes internet networking equipment, becomes the world's most valuable company on March 27, 2000, at $555.5 billion, ahead of Microsoft [16]. After the dot-com bubble bursts, the stock then loses nearly 90% of its value [17].
It took until December 10, 2025 for Cisco to regain its record close: a price that builds in too much hope can take years to be justified [18].

Paris stock market: Hermès loses 5% and drags luxury down, as fear of an AI crash raises concerns about spending by wealthy Americans

On Tuesday, November 17, the CAC 40 lost 1.62%, to 8,216.78 points. Hermès finished at the bottom, at −5.11%, ahead of Kering (−3.53%) and LVMH (−2.72%). On top of a still disappointing China, investors fear that the fall in AI stocks will make wealthy Americans poorer, the only luxury customers still growing [1][3].
At Tuesday's close, Hermès fell 5.11%, to €1,280.50, the biggest decline on the CAC 40. Kering fell 3.53%, to €178.36, and LVMH 2.72%, to €393 [1][12].
The CAC 40 lost 135.22 points, or 1.62%, to 8,216.78 points: tech fell again ahead of Nvidia's results, released that same evening [1].
In Europe, the Stoxx 600 index fell 1.75%, to 650.72 points: its biggest one-day drop since March 20. European tech stocks fell 3.9% [4][5].
European luxury stocks lost about 2% on average. Moncler fell 4.3%, to its lowest in four years [3].
"If markets remain volatile and weak, luxury consumer sentiment could suffer, and American customers are the only ones driving growth right now," warns Jelena Sokolova, an analyst at Morningstar [3].

China is still a drag: "the sector continues to suffer from weak demand in China," sums up an XTB analyst quoted by AFP [1]. On Monday, Morgan Stanley said it was "underweight" on luxury in its 2027 outlook for European equities, because of softer Chinese demand [3].
Investors took refuge in government bonds: France's borrowing rate fell to 4.88%, from 4.96% the day before [1][2].
Key takeaway: luxury, a heavyweight of the Paris stock market, now depends on a single engine, wealthy Americans, and that engine is tied to the health of AI stocks [3].

Since Chinese customers slowed down, LVMH, Hermès and Kering have bet on American consumers made richer by the AI and tech boom [3]. But Nvidia, the symbol of this boom, has dropped from first to third place among the world's largest companies by market value and has lost more than $1,000 billion in value since late October [1]. Washington has also restricted China's access to AI chips, which fueled concerns [13].
The luxury customer base is shrinking: according to analyst Luca Solca, the high cost of living has pushed many buyers out of the market, and brands are selling more to the same people [3].

Hermès was already weakened: on October 22, the stock fell about 8%, to €1,248, after quarterly revenue of €4.10 billion, below the €4.13 billion expected, with zero growth in Asia-Pacific excluding Japan [6][7].

Luxury carries a lot of weight in the CAC 40: if you have a stock savings plan or a life insurance policy invested in equities, these declines affect you. Remember the link: an AI slump in New York can slow handbag sales in Paris, because the customers are the same.

How it works: the wealth effect, or why AI is pulling down Hermès bags

The very wealthy hold a large share of their fortune in stocks. When the market rises, they feel richer and spend more, even without selling: this is "the wealth effect". When it falls, the opposite happens. The AI boom has made many Americans richer, and luxury brands have benefited [3]. If AI stocks fall, investors expect fewer purchases of bags, watches or jewelry, and they sell luxury stocks even before sales drop: the stock market runs on expectations. On the same day, they buy government bonds, seen as safer; as their price rises, their yield falls, which is why the French rate went from 4.96% to 4.88% [1].
Past cases: when China shakes, or lifts, luxury in Paris
August 12, 2015
China devalues its currency, the yuan: the CAC 40 plunges 3.4% in one session, LVMH loses 5.46%, to €155.85, and Kering 2.52% [10].
The very next day, Paris rebounds 1.25% and luxury recovers, despite a third devaluation in three days: a sudden shock does not always last [11].
September 24-26, 2024
China's central bank announces its biggest stimulus plan since Covid. On September 26, after a meeting of Chinese leaders, LVMH jumps 9.9%, Kering 9.6% and Hermès 9.1% [8].
In early October, with no new announcements from Beijing, hopes fade and luxury stocks fall again: the sector reacts very strongly to the slightest signal from China [9].
October 22, 2026
Hermès falls about 8%, to €1,248, after quarterly sales of €4.10 billion, below expectations; its chief financial officer calls the Chinese market "very difficult" [6][7].
Even the sector's strongest brand can no longer escape the Chinese slowdown, which makes luxury all the more dependent on American customers [3][6].

news.2026-11-18-suisse-ubs-regles-capita: Switzerland: UBS is set to lose its standoff over capital rules and is considering its future in the country

According to sources cited on Tuesday, November 17, UBS is preparing to give in on its long battle against new Swiss rules that require it to hold much more capital behind its foreign subsidiaries. Parliament could adopt these rules as early as December [1][2].
The government wants foreign subsidiaries to be 100% covered by the highest-quality capital [2].
The Council of States, the upper house, voted 29 to 16 for a 90% compromise, still well above what the bank holds today [1].
UBS now expects only symbolic concessions and plans to present its options in early February, along with its results, including a possible move abroad [1].
Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter played down this threat: a study by her ministry finds that a move to the United States would not be simple [1].
Key takeaway: UBS became a giant after taking over Credit Suisse [4]. This capital is a safety cushion: the thicker it is, the better the bank can absorb losses on its own in a crisis.
For the bank, these rules would lock up part of its profits and reduce the money available to buy back its own shares, a way of rewarding its shareholders [1][2].
UBS manages money for clients around the world, including in France. A better-protected bank reduces the risk of a crisis spreading to other European banks.

news.2026-11-18-argentine-malouines-prin: Falklands: Argentina calls Princess Anne's visit "provocative", amid a legal battle over the islands' oil

On Tuesday, November 17, Argentina's foreign ministry denounced the visit to the Falklands by Princess Anne, sister of King Charles III. Buenos Aires sees it as a "provocation", at a time when the United Kingdom is moving ahead with oil production around the islands [1][2].
For Argentina, the princess's activities are part of the "illegal British occupation" of the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands [1][2].

Pablo Quirno's ministry links the visit to the "unilateral" exploitation of hydrocarbons and points out that it has taken the matter to an international tribunal for the law of the sea, from which it is seeking urgent measures [2][3].
Buenos Aires is asking London to resume negotiations on sovereignty, as called for by a 1965 UN resolution [2].
The princess arrived on November 9 and is due to stay until November 20 [3].

Key takeaway: the protest is not new. Back in 2022, Alberto Fernández's government rejected a visit by Princess Anne with an identical statement [1]. Javier Milei, although close to the West, keeps the same line.
The real issue is oil. Argentina is challenging British drilling off the islands before international courts, and this issue could strain relations between London and Buenos Aires [2][3].
The Falklands seem far away, but the issue involves oil and the law of the sea, the same rules that govern France's overseas maritime zones.
